task_statement:
Research question (as posed on 2026-08-08, in the area of structural roles and influence):
Cut-heavy shapers' roles travel better than drive-heavy ones.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)
- NBA 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21; partial before)
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.
- Units available to a study of this question (as recorded): n=24

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

methodological_questions: defining player roles based on play-type data
measuring player impact after team change
controlling for confounding factors in player movement
sample size for player movement studies

historical_evidence.finding: Teams and players differ in how often H2 trigger possessions land on the engine's BEST vs AVOID counter. Team AVOID% ranges 50.6% (ORL) to 6.8% (SAC); team BEST% 0.0%-15.8%.
V5 player routing picks players with higher observed PPP than V4 routing. 8 divergences, 0 scoreable, 8 unscored (player missing from Neo4j); hit rate n/a.

The team-level BEST vs AVOID gap holds when H2 possessions are filtered to initiating player. Mean gap (n>=10 each tier) +0.427 PPP. Mean BEST 1.347 (38 players) vs AVOID 0.920 (94 players). Stars mean gap +0.542 (n=15) vs role +0.428 (n=16). Only 3 players clear n>=30 both tiers (all BOS: White +0.864, Brown +0. [cut; read_family for the full text]

Play-type PPP (especially DRIVE) declines as a playoff series progresses, so DRIVE is a good early-series call. Result: DRIVE 0.889 -> 0.949 (+0.060); CUT +0.114; PNR +0.087; PULL_UP -0.077; POST_UP -0.032.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Hypothesis testing for player tier tendency
failed_approaches.why: No outcome test; player samples 10-178 possessions.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Comparing V4 vs V5 player routing direct scoring
failed_approaches.why: A_unanswerable (question not answerable with the data or design); [prior work]; RISK:DRIFT_NONSTATIONARITY; RISK:SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER. Scoreable 0 of 8; V5 mostly routed to 'team' rather than a player.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Analyzing player-level BEST vs AVOID PPP gap for a sufficient number of players
failed_approaches.why: [prior work]; RISK:SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER. Pooled player gap +0.427 in the same direction as the team gap; most star cells are below the n>=30 gate.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Identifying a clear signal for play-type PPP change across playoff series game buckets
failed_approaches.why: E_unclear (mechanism unclear from [prior work]); [prior work]. 'NO CLEAR SIGNAL - DRIVE PPP is stable or improves across the series'; observational with selection caveats.

evidence_establishes: Player-level analysis of offensive tendencies and their associated Points Per Possession (PPP) is feasible.
Individual player sample sizes for specific play types can be very small, making robust conclusions difficult for many players.
Play-type PPP (including DRIVE and CUT) can be quantified and shows variation in different contexts (e.g., across playoff series progression).
Methodological risks such as SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER, DRIFT_NONSTATIONARITY, and selection/regression to the mean are common in player-centric studies.
evidence_does_not_establish: A standardized or robust method for classifying 'cut-heavy' vs 'drive-heavy' shapers.
A clear methodology for measuring the 'travel better' aspect of player roles, specifically how to quantify role portability or impact changes after a team change.
The typical sample size of players who change teams and fit specific play-type heavy roles.
Specific confounding factors relevant to player role portability other than general selection bias and regression to the mean.
own_inferences: The 'n=24 units' refers to the number of teams or similar high-level observational units, not directly to the number of players who changed teams and fit the shaper categories.

The primary challenge will be to identify a sufficient sample of players who are clearly 'cut-heavy' or 'drive-heavy' and have also changed teams across the available seasons, while controlling for team context.
uncertainties: The precise definition and thresholds for 'cut-heavy' and 'drive-heavy' shapers using the available play-type data.
The exact number of players who meet the criteria of changing teams and being classifiable as 'cut-heavy' or 'drive-heavy' shapers.
How to operationalize 'travel better' beyond simple PPP changes, e.g., considering usage rate, team offensive efficiency, or role within the new team context.
The specific confounding factors related to player movement (e.g., player age, contract status, reason for trade/signing, quality of new/old teammates) that need to be controlled.

historical_effect.explanation: The historical evidence, particularly [prior work][prior work] and [prior work][prior work], strongly highlights pervasive sample size limitations (RISK:SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER) when analyzing individual player-level data, especially when specific play-type thresholds are applied. This significantly lowered the estimated probability of testability and power. It also emphasized the need for careful definition of player roles and outcome metrics (PPP is a viable metric but context matters per [prior work][prior work]). The historical context reinforces the need for a very robust player classification and a clear methodological approach to account for small samples and confounding factors, leading to a decision to proceed with significant methodological changes to manage these risks.

blocking_constraints.text: The number of players who fit specific 'cut-heavy' or 'drive-heavy' definitions AND change teams across the available seasons is likely to be very small, making it difficult to achieve statistical power for comparing the two groups. Prior studies ([prior work][prior work], [prior work][prior work]) showed severe sample size limitations for player-level analysis.

Player movement is not random. Players change teams for various reasons (e.g., declining performance, contract disputes, team strategy, role changes) which can confound the assessment of 'portability'. The quality of old and new teammates, coaching, and system fit are significant confounders.

prior_work.summary: No prior work directly addressed the question of cut-heavy vs drive-heavy shaper role portability across teams. However, related studies provided insights into player-level analysis challenges, specifically concerning sample size for specific play-type categories and the measurement of play-type efficiency (PPP).

risks.text: The number of players who are clearly identifiable as 'cut-heavy' or 'drive-heavy' shapers and have changed teams during the observed period may be too small to draw statistically significant conclusions.

Player movement is highly confounded by factors such as player age, skill decline/improvement, team quality (old vs new), coaching schemes, and specific role changes, all of which can influence post-move performance independently of the 'shaper' type.

Defining 'cut-heavy' and 'drive-heavy' shapers objectively and reliably from play-type data, especially for players with lower usage, might be challenging. The stability of these classifications season-to-season for the same player is also a concern.

Basketball strategies and player roles evolve over time, and a player's role might change not just due to team change but also due to league-wide trends or personal development/decline. This can affect the comparability of roles across seasons.

Players who change teams might often be doing so after a particularly good or bad season, leading to regression to the mean in their subsequent performance, which could be misattributed to role portability.

design.estimand: The difference in average change in offensive impact (measured by Offensive PPP differential) between players classified as 'cut-heavy shapers' and 'drive-heavy shapers' after changing teams, controlling for player and team covariates.
design.unit: Player-season pairs, comparing performance before and after a team change.
design.sample: All players from the 2022-23 through 2025-26 NBA seasons who meet the following criteria: 1. Changed teams between two consecutive seasons. 2. Played at least 500 possessions in both the season before and the season after the team change. 3. Had at least 100 'cut' possessions and 100 'drive' possessions in the season prior to the team change. 4. Classified as 'cut-heavy' if their 'cut' possessions account for >X% of their total non-transition offensive possessions and 'drive-heavy' if their 'drive' possessions account for >Y% (thresholds X and Y to be determined based on data distribution to ensure sufficient sample sizes and clear distinction).
design.power: A power analysis will be conducted once the sample size of eligible players is determined. Given anticipated small sample sizes, the study will focus on effect size estimation and confidence intervals rather than solely p-values. If the sample size is critically low (e.g., <20 players per group), the study will pivot to a descriptive analysis of observed trends and individual player case studies.
design.controls: Control for player age, prior season's total PPP, prior season's usage rate, new team's offensive rating (prior season), old team's offensive rating (prior season), and whether the player was a starter. A difference-in-differences approach or a fixed-effects model (if multiple team changes exist for some players) will be considered to control for player-specific effects. Match players on key characteristics if feasible to create more comparable groups.
design.falsification: The primary hypothesis is that cut-heavy roles travel better. A falsification would involve finding no significant difference in portability, or that drive-heavy roles travel equally well or better. A secondary falsification would be if the classification of 'cut-heavy'/'drive-heavy' does not correlate with expected stylistic differences in play.
design.multiplicity: No multiple hypothesis tests are planned for the primary estimand. If thresholds for 'cut-heavy'/'drive-heavy' are tuned, this will be done carefully with sensitivity analysis to avoid p-hacking. Any exploratory analyses of different outcome metrics or subgroups will be clearly labeled as such.
design.decision_rule: The hypothesis will be considered supported if the confidence interval for the estimated difference in PPP change (cut-heavy vs drive-heavy) is positive and sufficiently far from zero (effect size determined a priori as meaningful, e.g., >0.05 PPP) with a p-value < 0.1 (due to expected small sample size challenges). Otherwise, it will be considered not supported or inconclusive.
design.data_version: NBA 2022-23 to 2025-26 regular season and playoffs. Play-by-play data, substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes, box-score summary, and derived play-type possession records from [source] database.
